Decompose differences in mortality by age, cause and subgroup

Source: R/derive-decompose.R
mt_decompose.Rd

Splits the difference in a mortality summary between two sets of rates into contributions of ages, causes of death and population subgroups. It is a post-processing step for observed data, forecasts, or both:

Usage

mt_decompose(
  x,
  y = NULL,
  var = NULL,
  ref = NULL,
  periods = NULL,
  quantity = c("life_expectancy", "prob_dying", "asr", "crude_rate"),
  method = NULL,
  cause = NULL,
  groups = NULL,
  hierarchy = NULL,
  composition = NULL,
  observed = c("data", "fitted", "poisson"),
  pairing = c("independent", "draw"),
  at = NULL,
  to = NULL,
  standard = "esp2013",
  per = 1e+05,
  exposure = NULL,
  n_steps = 20,
  n_draws = 1,
  probs = c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975),
  seed = 1,
  ...
)

# S3 method for class 'mt_decomposition'
summary(
  object,
  by = c("component", "group", "age", "cause"),
  probs = object$probs,
  change = NULL,
  ...
)

Arguments

x

An mt_data object (observed) or an mt_draws object (forecast).

y

Optional second mt_data or mt_draws object with the same age grid and strata.

var, ref

Stratum variable and its reference level for comparisons between strata.

periods

Years to compare (see Details). Defaults: the last year for comparisons between strata or objects; for changes, the first and last observed year of data, or the last observed and the last forecast year of draws.

quantity

"life_expectancy", "prob_dying", "asr", "crude_rate", or a function f(m, age) that takes a matrix of rates [age, n] (ages of the grid, age the mt_axis) and returns n values.

method

"arriaga", "horiuchi", "stepwise" or "kitagawa" (default: "arriaga" for life expectancy, "kitagawa" for the crude rate, "horiuchi" otherwise and for pooled composition).

cause

Stratum variable holding causes of death, whose rates add up to all causes.

groups

Stratum variable holding population subgroups.

hierarchy

An mt_hierarchy() that declares total and group levels of cause and groups (default: the hierarchy stored in x or y).

composition

"radix" or "pooled"; required with groups (see Subgroups).

observed

How observed years held in forecast draws enter: "data" (observed rates), "fitted" (the model's fitted rates) or "poisson" (Poisson draws of the observed deaths). See Observed and forecast years.

pairing

"independent" or "draw": how the draws of x and y are paired.

at

Starting age (life expectancy at at; lower bound of prob_dying); default the first grid age.

to

Upper age for "prob_dying".

standard, per

Standard population and multiplier for "asr" (see asr()); per also scales "crude_rate".

exposure

Exposures for forecast years [age, stratum] or [age, period, stratum] (see mt_deaths()).

n_steps

Number of steps of "horiuchi".

n_draws

For mt_data: 1 (the observed rates) or the number of Poisson draws.

probs

Quantile levels of the summaries.

seed

Seed of Poisson draws and of the shuffling of y.

...

Passed to the life table (ax, open, k, see life_table()) for life expectancy.

object

An mt_decomposition object.

by

Variables of the contributions to keep ("component", "group", "age", "cause"); the others are summed path by path. NULL gives the totals.

change

Two periods: the change of each comparison between them (for comparisons between strata or objects in several periods), formed path by path.

Value

An mt_decomposition object. summary() returns contributions summed (path by path) over the variables not in by, with mean and quantiles; summary(by = NULL) returns one row per comparison (its number in comparison) with the values in the two populations, their difference (mean and quantiles), the jump-off share where it applies, the sum of the contributions and the largest difference between the two over draws (max_residual). summary(change = c(p1, p2)) decomposes the change between two periods of comparisons between strata or objects (for example of a gap), path by path. print() shows the totals.

Details

  • with var and ref, each level of a stratum variable is compared with a reference level (for example the deprivation gap Q5 - Q1 in each sex), in each of periods;

  • with y, y is compared with x for matching strata and periods (two forecasts, or observed data and a forecast);

  • otherwise the change from the first of periods to each later one is decomposed for every stratum. For forecast draws, periods may mix observed years (the training data held in the draws) and forecast years.

Forecasts are decomposed draw by draw, so every contribution has an interval, and sums over ages, causes or subgroups (summary()) are formed path by path. Observed data give the decomposition of the observed rates (n_draws = 1) or, with n_draws > 1, Poisson draws of the deaths as in mt_observed(). Totals and contributions are means over draws; summary() adds quantiles.

Observed and forecast years

Forecast draws hold the observed rates of their training years. A change from an observed year to a forecast year then contains the step from the observed to the model's fitted rates of that year (the jump-off, see mt_jump_off()) and the sampling noise of the observed year, besides the forecast change itself. The totals report the jump-off share (jump_off). observed = "fitted" uses the fitted rates of observed years, so that the decomposition describes the model's change alone; observed = "poisson" uses Poisson draws of the observed deaths, so that their sampling uncertainty enters the intervals.

Two objects (y) are compared draw by draw. Draws of different models are independent, so by default (pairing = "independent") the draws of y are shuffled before pairing; draws of models with the same seed would otherwise share their random numbers and give intervals that are too narrow. Use pairing = "draw" when y is derived from the draws of x (for example a reconciliation of the same draws).

Methods

  • "arriaga" (life expectancy): the symmetric Arriaga decomposition, the average of the decompositions from 1 to 2 and (with the sign reversed) from 2 to 1, computed on the package's life table (... passes ax and open to it). Causes get the age-specific contribution in proportion to their rate differences (an implied sensitivity, Riffe et al. 2024, eqs. 12-13 of the working paper); where the all-cause difference is close to zero, the sensitivity is a numerical derivative at the average rates. Exact.

  • "horiuchi" (any quantity): the line-integral method of Horiuchi, Wilmoth and Pletcher (2008) with n_steps steps; exact up to a small discretisation error, reported in the totals.

  • "stepwise" (any quantity): stepwise replacement (Andreev, Shkolnikov and Begun 2002) from the youngest to the oldest age, averaged over both directions of the comparison; with causes, all causes of an age are replaced before the next age (DemoDecomp and LEdecomp replace cause by cause, which changes the split between causes slightly). Exact; results depend on the order. Arriaga's decomposition from 1 to 2 is stepwise replacement from the oldest to the youngest age, so for life expectancy without causes the two symmetric versions are identical.

  • "kitagawa" (crude death rate): the rate effect (age-specific rates at the average age structure) and the composition effect (age structure at the average rates) of Kitagawa (1955). Exact.

Draws whose rates give no valid life table (for example rates far above any observed value, see the warning of mt_forecast()) are left out with a warning, and a warning reports contributions that do not add up to the difference.

Subgroups

With groups, the populations being compared consist of the levels of a stratum variable, and the decomposition separates the effect of their composition. composition must be chosen, because the two options describe different quantities:

  • "radix" (Riffe, Tursun-zade and Trias Llimós 2024, "Arriaga meets Kitagawa"): life expectancy (or the probability of dying) of the population is the mean of the subgroups' values, weighted by their population shares at the starting age (at), as when subgroup life tables are blended at the radix ("current conditions" in the terms of Vaupel 2002, which the authors use). A Kitagawa decomposition of that mean gives one composition effect and, for each subgroup, its difference times its average share, which is split by age (and cause) with method. The authors state that this holds when membership is fixed from the starting age on and later shares change only through mortality: education from age 30 or 35, sex, country of birth. It does not hold for areas such as deprivation quintiles or regions, between which people move and which are reclassified.

  • "pooled": the quantity of the pooled rates, which weight the subgroup rates by their population shares at each age (the rates of the aggregate strata, as published for whole populations; "current rates"). The rates of every subgroup, age and cause and the shares at every age are the parameters of a "horiuchi" (default) or "stepwise" decomposition; the composition effects are reported by age, summed over subgroups, whose separate composition terms are not identified. With many subgroups, causes and draws this takes minutes; lower n_steps or the number of draws for a first look.

Shares come from the exposures: of each observed year, and for forecast years from exposure (default: the last observed year, so composition does not change in the forecast unless exposures, for example a population projection, are given).

Totals among causes and groups

Levels of cause and groups that are totals of the others (for example the cause "all" or the region "Germany") must not be counted as parts. They are left out when the hierarchy declares them: hierarchy, or what the object records, the total of mt_group_levels() (total, also in fits and draws of such data) and the hierarchy of mt_aggregate_strata() or reconciled(). A level that equals the sum of the others in the observed deaths without being declared stops the decomposition.

References

Arriaga EE (1984). Measuring and explaining the change in life expectancies. Demography 21(1): 83-96. doi:10.2307/2061029

Kitagawa EM (1955). Components of a difference between two rates. Journal of the American Statistical Association 50(272): 1168-1194. doi:10.1080/01621459.1955.10501299

Andreev EM, Shkolnikov VM, Begun AZ (2002). Algorithm for decomposition of differences between aggregate demographic measures and its application to life expectancies, healthy life expectancies, parity-progression ratios and total fertility rates. Demographic Research 7: 499-522.

Horiuchi S, Wilmoth JR, Pletcher SD (2008). A decomposition method based on a model of continuous change. Demography 45(4): 785-801. doi:10.1353/dem.0.0033

Riffe T, Tursun-zade R, Trias Llimós S (2024). Arriaga meets Kitagawa. Life expectancy decomposition with population subgroups. MPIDR Working Paper WP-2024-029. doi:10.4054/MPIDR-WP-2024-029 . Published in Geographical Analysis (2026), doi:10.1111/gean.70033 .

Vaupel JW (2002). Life expectancy at current rates vs. current conditions: a reflexion stimulated by Bongaarts and Feeney's "How long do we live?". Demographic Research 7: 365-378.

Examples

x <- mt_example(deaths = "single", years = 2000:2015)
# change 2000-2015 in life expectancy at 30, by age, per sex
d <- mt_decompose(x, periods = c(2000, 2015), at = 30)
d
#> <mt_decomposition> life expectancy at 30, method arriaga; 2 comparison(s), 1 draw
#>    comparison    sex   from     to from_value to_value difference
#>         <int> <char> <char> <char>      <num>    <num>      <num>
#> 1:          1 female   2000   2015     53.853   55.443      1.590
#> 2:          2   male   2000   2015     48.585   50.584      1.998
#>    sum_contributions max_residual
#>                <num>        <num>
#> 1:             1.590      4.9e-15
#> 2:             1.998      6.0e-15
summary(d, by = "age")[1:5]
#>       sex   from     to    age        mean      q0.025        q0.5      q0.975
#>    <char> <char> <char> <char>       <num>       <num>       <num>       <num>
#> 1: female   2000   2015     30 0.004438172 0.004438172 0.004438172 0.004438172
#> 2: female   2000   2015     31 0.018028104 0.018028104 0.018028104 0.018028104
#> 3: female   2000   2015     32 0.013227430 0.013227430 0.013227430 0.013227430
#> 4: female   2000   2015     33 0.005466655 0.005466655 0.005466655 0.005466655
#> 5: female   2000   2015     34 0.019223513 0.019223513 0.019223513 0.019223513
# the sex gap in forecast years, with intervals, and its change
fc <- mt_forecast(mt_fit(lee_carter(), x), h = 10, n_draws = 100, seed = 1)
g <- mt_decompose(fc, var = "sex", ref = "male", periods = c(2016, 2025), at = 30)
summary(g, by = NULL)
#>    comparison   from     to period from_value to_value difference
#>         <int> <char> <char>  <num>      <num>    <num>      <num>
#> 1:          1   male female   2016    50.7036 55.53837   4.834771
#> 2:          2   male female   2025    51.8860 56.43574   4.549737
#>    difference_q0.025 difference_q0.5 difference_q0.975 sum_contributions
#>                <num>           <num>             <num>             <num>
#> 1:          4.598310        4.822230          5.116275          4.834771
#> 2:          3.524936        4.490365          5.738382          4.549737
#>    max_residual
#>           <num>
#> 1: 7.105427e-15
#> 2: 7.105427e-15
summary(g, by = "age", change = c(2016, 2025))[1:5]
#>      from     to       period    age          mean       q0.025          q0.5
#>    <char> <char>       <char> <char>         <num>        <num>         <num>
#> 1:   male female 2016 to 2025     30 -0.0024570174 -0.006658112 -0.0028170201
#> 2:   male female 2016 to 2025     31 -0.0022004343 -0.006999818 -0.0025019450
#> 3:   male female 2016 to 2025     32 -0.0052739998 -0.010412948 -0.0057943852
#> 4:   male female 2016 to 2025     33 -0.0035476847 -0.007691005 -0.0039742845
#> 5:   male female 2016 to 2025     34 -0.0001011823 -0.004194642 -0.0000860906
#>         q0.975
#>          <num>
#> 1: 0.002982563
#> 2: 0.004271740
#> 3: 0.001939599
#> 4: 0.001811163
#> 5: 0.005137142
# observed 2015 against the forecast of 2025, with the jump-off share
mt_decompose(fc, periods = c(2015, 2025), at = 30)
#> <mt_decomposition> life expectancy at 30, method arriaga; 2 comparison(s), means over 100 draws
#>    comparison    sex   from     to from_value to_value difference
#>         <int> <char> <char> <char>      <num>    <num>      <num>
#> 1:          1 female   2015   2025     55.443   56.436      0.993
#> 2:          2   male   2015   2025     50.584   51.886      1.302
#>    difference_q0.025 difference_q0.5 difference_q0.975 jump_off
#>                <num>           <num>             <num>    <num>
#> 1:             0.442           1.005             1.523   -0.008
#> 2:             0.251           1.337             2.231    0.024
#>    sum_contributions max_residual
#>                <num>        <num>
#> 1:             0.993      4.3e-15
#> 2:             1.302      6.9e-15
#> jump_off: part of the difference due to observed instead of fitted rates in observed years of the draws
#> (see mt_jump_off()); observed = "fitted" decomposes the model's change alone.
